title: Chemical intuition: reading a CdSe synthesis mechanistically
anchor: Murray, Norris and Bawendi (1993), CdSe Methods 1 and 2
scope: Seven interpretive cards for a material-centered page. Later research contextualizes the historical methods; it neither supplies missing recipe fields nor measures the original specimens retrospectively.

cards.title: Why inject into a hot coordinating medium?
cards.takeaway: Injection changes the reaction rapidly; a brief mixing event does not by itself prove a brief nucleation event.

original.text: The 1993 authors propose that rapid injection produces a nucleation burst, followed by reagent depletion and cooling that suppress further nucleation; reheating supports growth.

later.text: Prins and colleagues observed nucleation overlapping growth for about 15-20% of reaction time in their CdSe system using in situ X-ray scattering.

cards.interpretation: Keep the observed injection operation separate from the proposed nucleation mechanism.
cards.caveat: The later duration is system-specific; it neither establishes the 1993 timing nor invalidates every burst-nucleation model.
cards.outlook: Test mechanism transfer using particle-number and size trajectories alongside the actual mixing and thermal history.

cards.title: Why distinguish Method 1 from Method 2?
cards.takeaway: The selenium source controls more than the amount of selenium supplied.

original.text: For CdSe, Method 1 uses TOPSe; Method 2 replaces it with bis(trimethylsilyl)selenium. The authors prefer phosphine chalcogenides for ease of preparation and stability and discuss prior dealkylsilylation chemistry for the silyl route.

later.text: Owen and colleagues tracked precursor disappearance by phosphorus NMR and CdSe formation by absorption. In their Cd-ODPA system, precursor conversion limited nucleation/growth; changing phosphine-selenide reactivity changed particle number and final size.

cards.interpretation: Equal elemental feed does not guarantee equal delivery of growth material over time.
cards.caveat: This study does not establish a TOPSe-versus-silylselenide rate ranking for the historical methods. A more reactive precursor does not universally mean a larger particle.
cards.outlook: Measure conversion before treating precursor swaps as equivalent recipe substitutions.

cards.title: How can growth narrow the size distribution?
cards.takeaway: Average size and distribution width are separate outcomes governed by competing processes.

original.text: The authors describe growth as consistent with Ostwald ripening and adjust temperature using absorption linewidths as a rough indicator of distribution width.

later.text: Prins and colleagues found focusing faster than diffusion-limited predictions. They interpreted it through strongly size-dependent surface reactivity; kinetic simulations showed that such superfocusing can coexist with extended nucleation.
later.locator: Abstract; focusing experiments and kinetic simulations

cards.interpretation: Follow particle number, size and width together; a narrow final sample does not uniquely identify its growth mechanism.
cards.caveat: Do not equate every narrowing event with Ostwald ripening, or turn historical optical feedback into a calibrated temperature-to-size rule.
cards.outlook: Compare growth models against the same time-resolved observations and quantify where their predictions separate.

cards.title: Why can two TOPO supplies behave differently?
cards.takeaway: Minor components can change precursor chemistry and morphology.

original.text: The 1993 preparation purifies TOPO by distillation and describes the coordinating medium as controlling growth, stabilizing dispersion and passivating the surface.

later.text: Wang and Buhro found dots with added DOPO but rods with DOPA in a TDPA/TOPO system. Their NMR-supported interpretation connects these outcomes to secondary phosphine formation and altered precursor-conversion/nucleation kinetics. Outcomes differed in the oleic-acid system.
later.locator: Abstract; Results, Morphology control and growth kinetics; Conclusion

cards.interpretation: Record reagent composition and pretreatment, not just the name on the bottle.
cards.caveat: This does not identify impurities in Murray's purified TOPO or prove that a named additive always produces one shape.
cards.outlook: Test whether measured reagent fingerprints improve prediction across lots and laboratories.

cards.title: Does the recipe name reveal the surface ligands?
cards.takeaway: A solvent/ligand label is not a measured inventory of the final surface.

original.text: The article calls its products TOP/TOPO capped and reports that pyridine exchange changes dispersibility and slightly changes the size distribution.

later.text: Kopping and Patten used ligand displacement and phosphorus NMR to identify multiple bound phosphorus species in CdSe made with technical-grade TOPO. Controlled-additive experiments identified phosphonic acid and its condensation product as predominant surface ligands in particular preparations.

cards.interpretation: Keep synthesis ingredients, post-workup surface composition and measurement state as separate records.
cards.caveat: The later ligand inventory cannot be assigned retrospectively to the 1993 particles, whose TOPO was distilled.
cards.outlook: Pair surface-sensitive measurements with optical measurements on the same aliquot to test surface-property links.

cards.title: Why are phase and shape not temperature labels?
cards.takeaway: The surface environment can help select atomic stacking as well as morphology.

original.text: TEM and XRD modeling support slightly prolate, predominantly wurtzite CdSe with stacking faults. The authors caution against a pure wurtzite/zincblende label; surface disorder is compatible with, but not uniquely determined by, their diffraction data.
original.locator: pp. 8710-8714, TEM, Structural Simulations and structural summary

later.text: Gao and Peng experimentally found that cadmium carboxylate ligands favored zinc blende whereas long-chain cadmium phosphonate ligands favored wurtzite in their systems, with effects during both nucleation and growth.

cards.interpretation: Phase prediction needs ligand/precursor context, and structural evidence should retain stacking disorder rather than force a binary label.
cards.caveat: This is not a universal ligand lookup table or evidence that Methods 1 and 2 have different phases. The smallest approximately 1.2-nm clusters lack a meaningful bulk-polytype assignment in the original paper.
cards.outlook: Test phase-selectivity models while jointly tracking size, surface chemistry and fault-sensitive structural measurements.

cards.title: Why is the retained fraction part of the chemistry?
cards.takeaway: Purification can change which particles constitute the reported sample.

original.text: The paper distinguishes removal of gray Cd/Se-rich byproducts from size-selective precipitation. Its Figure 1 example narrows a population from about 3.5 nm with 10% spread to about 3.7 nm with 5% spread by fractionation.
original.locator: pp. 8707-8708, Isolation/Purification, Size-Selective Precipitation and Figure 1

cards.interpretation: A narrower final distribution may reflect selection as well as growth. Keep the crude population and each retained fraction connected to their measurements.
cards.caveat: Figure 1 is an example, not a universal purification-cycle count or proof that every batch achieves the same width. Its sample is not automatically identical to the TEM or PL examples.
cards.outlook: Report recovered yield and discarded fractions when evaluating whether a synthesis truly improved uniformity.

editorial_guardrails: Display original, later, interpretation and outlook labels visibly; attach source links to the corresponding claim rather than a single generic bibliography.
Use the six primary research sources above as the reading set; this is a selective historical-to-mechanistic explanation, not an exhaustive or latest-frontier survey.

Some full publisher pages were inaccessible; verification statements distinguish inspected local full text from indexed primary abstracts and passages. Do not say every later main article or supplement was fully read.

Do not present all related papers as direct citations of Murray 1993: source-to-source citation relationships were not comprehensively audited. The claims themselves are verified against the specified primary research records.
Do not insert later ligands, numerical conditions or mechanistic assumptions into the 1993 executable record.
Outlook questions are proposed research directions and may already have partial answers; none is claimed entirely novel.
No new experimental curves, ligand structures, rate constants or quantified predictions are generated by these cards.
